ablations.verdict: On the controlled set the best backend catches 9/9 sentences that contradict the measured indices; with the gate off all 9 reach the user. The deterministic backend costs nothing measurable (-98.8 ms, within run-to-run noise); adding NLI costs +6745.4 ms per query, 2.6x the unverified pipeline on this machine.
ablations.caveat: The end-to-end arm ran the learned tools (caption_v1, change_caption_v1, change_mask_v1, grounding_v1, landcover_v1, optsar_fusion_v1, rs_vqa_v1) on 8 routine queries over synthetic scenes. The deterministic backend flagged 0 of 22 sentences; with NLI, 6 of 22 were flagged in 5 answers (listed under flagged_examples). These are unlabelled, so a flag here is not by itself a caught error. The controlled arm, where contradictions are planted, is what measures what the gate catches.

ablations.name: agent vs monolith
ablations.question: Does config gating + plan validation prevent anything the same classifier would otherwise do?
ablations.verdict: The same classifier, ungated, selects an impossible task on 104/600 plans (17.3%) - change detection on a single image, fusion without SAR. Gated, the rate is 0/600. The structure, not the model, is what produces the guarantee.
ablations.caveat: This measures LEGALITY, not answer quality: the guards prevent impossible plans. Answer quality is measured separately - each deployed tool on its official test split (the table above) and routing on the held-out NL benchmark (evaluation/nl/).

ablations.name: triad (optical / SAR / fused)
ablations.question: Does optical-SAR fusion beat the better single modality?
ablations.verdict: Fusion beats optical alone: fused mIoU 0.4681 against 0.4467 (+0.0214; per-tile gain 95 % CI [+0.0057, +0.0124]), better on 66% of tiles. Zeroing the SAR input drops the fused head to 0.4090, so the gain comes from the SAR.
ablations.caveat: Per-pixel segmentation on WHU-OPT-SAR, split by scene (29 train / 7 validation scenes). The same 7 scenes also chose the epoch (fused mIoU), so the fused number carries a small selection bias; the gain is small in absolute terms. The earlier scene-level classification version of this ablation found no gain (-0.0064): at scene level either sensor alone can say 'there is water in this tile', so fusion only shows up per pixel.

ablations.name: two-track (specialist vs VLM)
ablations.question: Does the two-track split earn its complexity?

track_b (QLoRA VLM).note: not run here - needs the 4-bit base model and a GPU

ablations.verdict: Not answerable from what exists. The two tracks were trained and evaluated on DIFFERENT tasks and DIFFERENT splits - land-cover mAP on BigEarthNet against VQA accuracy on VRSBench - so no comparison between the numbers means anything.
ablations.caveat: What would make this a real ablation, stated so it can be built: one task both tracks can perform, on one split, with one metric. Land-cover classification is the natural choice - ask the VLM 'which of these 19 classes are present' on the same BigEarthNet test shard the specialist head is scored on. That is a Phase 3 run that has not happened, not a number that is missing.

note: Each arm reports its own status: measured end to end, measured offline from a training run, or not comparable with the missing run named. Four tables of equal apparent authority would have been the dishonest presentation.
